newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - UK media heavyweights team up for TV fight.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - UK media heavyweights team up for TV fight.

text.p: Three British broadcasting heavyweights will learn shortly if they have overcome a smaller cable rival in the fight to pioneer new television services available in every home.

Digital terrestrial television (DTT) means little to the average British viewer but its potential has tempted television giants British Sky Broadcasting Group Plc, Carlton Communications Plc and Granada Group Plc to team up in an unprecedented alliance.

The trio has formed the British Digital Broadcasting (BDB) consortium in a bid to secure three key DTT licences. It wants to launch 15 new subscription channels and has pledged to put up to 300 million pounds ($485 million) into the venture.

Pitted against them in a David and Goliath contest is the DTN consortium, owned by Nasdaq-listed NTL Inc. Nearly all NTL's activities are in Britain where it is the third largest group in the fledgling cable sector and owns a broadcast transmission network.
Satellite broadcaster BSkyB, in which Rupert Murdoch's News Corp is the main shareholder, dominates British pay TV while Carlton and Granada are two of the most successful commercial TV companies.
The trio have a combined stock market value of some 20 billion pounds --$32.5 billion -- which dwarfs NTL.
"There is a general industry perception that BDB is the invincible powerhouse consortium," says Dermot Nolan, technical director of media consultants Convergent Decisions Group.

Nolan believes the formation of BDB may come to be seen as a key event in the development of the British media. It meant that DTT was suddenly regarded as a viable proposition rather than a commercial non-starter.
"The emergence of BDB as a major bidder for DTT capacity left many City analysts, columnists, commentators and chief executives rapidly revising their opinions," he said.
WHAT WILL IT OFFER
So what will digital terrestrial television offer Britons, Europe's most avid watchers of the small screen?

DTT, a technology which Britain is pioneering, will allow viewers to receive more than 30 channels via a standard rooftop aerial, rather than the current five terrestrial channels. Picture quality will be enhanced and online services can also be created.
Viewers will however need one additional piece of kit in the form of a set-top box to decode signals. The box is expected to be subsidised down to a price of around 300 pounds.
"Going digital is the most important development for British television since the introduction of colour," Carlton chairman Michael Green said as his consortium launched its bid.

"By plugging in one simple set top box, viewers will be able to see all the existing terrestrial channels, new free channels, the latest movies, the best sport, the highest quality drama..., " added Green, who chairs BDB.
The channels will be broadcast on six blocks of frequencies known as "multiplexes" and licensed by the Independent Television Commission (ITC).
Existing terrestrial broadcasters such as the BBC and ITV have been given places on three multiplexes and plan to use the extra capacity to add new free channels.
BDB and DTN are contesting the other three multiplexes on which they plan to offer pay television.
The ITC is expected to award the licences later this month. It could decide to split the licences although this is considered the least likely option.
Its decision will be based on factors such as the ability to establish and maintain the service and appeal to a variety of tastes and interests. The services are expected on air by mid-1998.
DTN argues that the BDB bid would allow its three members to tighten their stranglehold on British television and do nothing to boost choice and variety.

"DTN brings new programming choices rather than the 'more of the same' on offer from BDB, and will provide competition for advertisers," DTN chief executive Jeremy Thorp wrote in the trade magazine Media Week.
DTN plans the movies and sport channels which are the staple diet of pay TV but has highlighted its commitment to educational programming and local-based programming.
It also plans to allow viewers to access services such as the Internet and home shopping and banking, claiming that the BDB bid underplays the potential for these services.
BSkyB'S COMMITMENT QUESTIONED
Another line of attack has been to question the commitment of BSkyB to DTT, given that the company has said it also plans to launch 200-channel digital satellite services into Britain late this year.
"DTN is the only bidder with an unambiguous and single-minded commitment to making a success of DTT," it said in a briefing paper.
"BSkyB have made it clear again and again that their first priority will be driving digital satellite transmission," it added.

BSkyB argues that the two digital services -- satellite and terrestrial -- are complementary. BDB plans to develop an add-on gadget which will mean its set-top boxes can also decode digital satellite signals.
BDB, which has secured first refusal on new BBC pay channels, believes its programme strength will guarantee the new service catches on.

"Our proposals bring together the U.K.'s best programme-makers -- the BBC, Carlton and Granada -- with the leading provider of sport and top Hollywood movies," BDB project leader Nigel Walmsley wrote in Media Week.
"It is these, rather than advanced interactive services, which will initially drive take-up," he added.
Walmsley stressed that BDB had the financial muscle to battle its way through the inevitable early problems for a business which must start from scratch.
"In broadcasting, big ideas usually need substantial financial resources. We have both," Walmsley said.
($ = 0.616 British Pounds)
